scenario.context: In Ravenmarch, Rowan can produce 10 copper or 4 rope per week. Halvard can produce 6 copper or 3 rope per week. Rowan is better at both and refuses to trade.
scenario.text: Rowan scoffs: 'I make more of everything. Why would I trade with Halvard?' Halvard looks dejected.
scenario.speaker_context: Rowan confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage.

structure.pattern_description: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, not absolute productivity. Even if one party is better at everything, both benefit from specializing where their opportunity cost is lowest and trading.
structure.formal_form: Rowan: OC of 1 rope = 2.5 copper. Halvard: OC of 1 rope = 2.0 copper. Since 2.0 < 2.5, Halvard has CA in rope; Rowan has CA in copper.
structure.why_right: Trade benefits do not require equal productivity. Specialization by comparative advantage increases total output and enables both parties to consume more.
structure.counterpoint: Transaction costs, transport risks, and strategic vulnerability can make self-sufficiency rational despite theoretical gains from trade.

assessment.identification_prompt: Rowan outproduces Halvard in both goods. Should they still trade? Calculate opportunity costs.

rubric.description: Player agrees Rowan has no reason to trade.
Player suspects trade could help but cannot calculate why.
Player calculates some opportunity costs but makes errors.
Player correctly identifies who has CA in which good.
Player calculates CA, proposes a beneficial trade ratio, and explains the logic.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Forget totals. What does Rowan sacrifice in copper to make one rope? Now ask the same for Halvard. Who sacrifices less?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What trade ratio between copper and rope would make both better off?

scenario.context: Sigrid, a apothecary in Grainfield, has 139 gold to buy iron ingots and lockpicks for an expedition. iron ingots cost 8 gold each (3 units of supply). lockpicks cost 6 gold each (5 units of protection). Need at least 24 supply and 9 protection.
scenario.text: '139 gold, no more. iron ingots: 8 gold, 3 supply each. lockpicks: 6 gold, 5 protection each. We need 24 supply and 9 protection minimum. What is the cheapest way to meet both needs?'
scenario.speaker_context: Sigrid wants to minimize cost subject to meeting minimum requirements.

structure.pattern_description: Maximize or minimize an objective subject to binding constraints. Sigrid must meet requirements at minimum cost within a fixed budget.
structure.formal_form: Min C = 8*A + 6*B s.t. 3*A >= 24, 5*B >= 9. A >= 8, B >= 2. Min cost = 76. Surplus = 63.
structure.why_right: Constrained optimization is the core microeconomic framework. Every agent faces scarce resources and must find the best feasible combination.
structure.counterpoint: Models assume known prices, divisible goods, and certain requirements. Real decisions involve uncertainty, lumpy goods, and changing prices.

assessment.identification_prompt: Find the minimum-cost purchase that meets 24 supply and 9 protection.

scenario.context: Cael, a furrier in Ashwick, sells tallow candles for 22 gold each. The cost of each additional unit rises: 10, 13, 16, 30, 31, 34, 36.
scenario.text: '22 gold per tallow candle. Costs keep rising: 10, 13, 16, 30, 31, 34, 36 gold for units 1 through 7. How many should I make?'
scenario.speaker_context: Cael needs to compare MB (22) to MC for each unit.

structure.pattern_description: Compare the marginal benefit to the marginal cost of each additional unit. Continue if MB >= MC; stop when MC > MB.
structure.formal_form: MB = 22 for each unit. MC = [10, 13, 16, 30, 31, 34, 36]. Produce while MB >= MC. Q* = 3. Total profit = 27.
structure.why_right: Marginal analysis prevents both underproduction (stopping too early) and overproduction (making units that cost more than they earn).
structure.counterpoint: Marginal analysis assumes you can adjust one unit at a time. When production is lumpy or irreversible, the framework needs adaptation.

assessment.identification_prompt: At 22 gold per unit with costs 10, 13, 16, 30, 31, 34, 36, how many should Cael produce?

structure.pattern_description: Compare the marginal benefit to the marginal cost of each additional unit. Continue if MB >= MC; stop when MC > MB.

scenario.context: Millhaven has 7 merchants who benefit from signal beacon fuel. The total cost is 104 gold per month (15 gold each). One merchant, Declan, proposes letting the others cover it.
scenario.text: '15 gold is 15 gold,' says Declan. 'If the other 6 pay, the signal beacon fuel happens and I save my share. The signal beacon fuel benefits me whether I pay or not.'
scenario.speaker_context: Declan identifies the free-rider incentive in a public goods problem.

structure.pattern_description: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable, creating a free-rider incentive: each agent benefits regardless of contribution. Individual rationality leads to collective underprovision.
structure.formal_form: Public good: non-rival, non-excludable. Each agent's dominant strategy is to free ride. If all free ride, good is not provided. N-player PD.
structure.why_wrong: Free riding is individually rational but collectively destructive. If universalized, the good is not provided and all are worse off.
structure.why_right: Recognizing the free-rider problem is the first step toward solutions: binding agreements, social enforcement, or centralized provision.
structure.counterpoint: Not all shared goods are public goods. Excludability and rivalry vary on a spectrum. Club goods (excludable but non-rival) avoid the free-rider problem.

assessment.identification_prompt: What happens if every merchant reasons like Declan? Why does this problem arise?

rubric.description: Player sees nothing wrong with Declan's reasoning.
Player senses collective failure but cannot explain the mechanism.
Player identifies under-provision but not the underlying properties.
Player identifies non-rivalry, non-excludability, and the PD structure.
Player identifies all elements and proposes solution mechanisms.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Declan doesn't pay and the rest do, Declan saves 15 gold. Now imagine all 7 think this way.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What mechanism could the merchants create to prevent free riding?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Declan is shrewd and unapologetic about self-interest.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: 'Why should I pay when the signal beacon fuel happens whether I chip in or not?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the problem and proposes a mechanism, the merchants form a binding charter.

scenario.context: The merchants of Northcrest have solved the free-rider problem for harbor dredging through social enforcement for years. But the town is growing, and new merchants arrive who have no social ties. Does the informal system still work at scale?
scenario.text: 'When there were five of us, shame kept everyone honest. Now there are twenty and half of them are strangers. Our old system is breaking down.'
scenario.speaker_context: Informal solutions to public goods problems scale poorly. At what point is formal governance needed?

structure.pattern_description: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable, creating a free-rider incentive: each agent benefits regardless of contribution. Individual rationality leads to collective underprovision.
structure.formal_form: As N grows: monitoring costs rise, social pressure weakens, marginal impact of each contribution falls. Transition to formal taxation/governance becomes necessary.
structure.why_wrong: Free riding is individually rational but collectively destructive. If universalized, the good is not provided and all are worse off.
structure.why_right: Recognizing the free-rider problem is the first step toward solutions: binding agreements, social enforcement, or centralized provision.
structure.counterpoint: Not all shared goods are public goods. Excludability and rivalry vary on a spectrum. Club goods (excludable but non-rival) avoid the free-rider problem.

assessment.identification_prompt: Why do informal free-rider solutions break down as group size grows? What institutional alternatives exist?

scenario.context: The berry thicket near Grainfield sustains 43 ore carts per season. 8 families share it. Recently, total extraction hit 71, exceeding the sustainable yield.
scenario.text: Zara hauls in a heavy load. 'If I leave these in the berry thicket, someone else takes them tomorrow. At least this way my family eats.' The elder notes extraction is 28 ore carts above sustainable levels.
scenario.speaker_context: Zara follows individually rational logic that leads to collective depletion.

structure.pattern_description: A common-pool resource is rival but non-excludable. Each user captures full private benefit of extraction but bears only a fraction of the depletion cost, driving overuse.
structure.formal_form: Common-pool resource: rival, non-excludable. Private MB of extra extraction > private MC (shared 1/8). Each overextracts. Total > sustainable yield 43.
structure.why_wrong: Individual rationality drives overextraction. The problem is structural, not moral — the incentive system is misaligned.
structure.why_right: Recognizing the commons structure points toward solutions: property rights, catch limits, or community governance.
structure.counterpoint: Not all commons are doomed. Ostrom documented successful community governance of shared resources without privatization or centralized control.

assessment.identification_prompt: Each family benefits from taking more, but the berry thicket is declining. What structural problem drives this?

rubric.description: Player blames individual greed without seeing the structure.
Player sees overharvesting but not the incentive asymmetry.
Player identifies individual incentive but not the rivalry/excludability properties.
Player identifies the tragedy of the commons structure fully.
Player identifies the structure and proposes governance solutions.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: When Zara takes one extra ore cart, who gets the benefit? Who bears the cost of depletion?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What governance mechanism could align individual incentives with sustainability?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Zara is pragmatic, not malicious — responding rationally to bad incentives.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: 'If I leave it, someone else takes it. At least my family benefits.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the commons problem and proposes governance, the families convene a council and establish catch limits.

scenario.context: The timber forest near Ashenmoor sustains 80 crates of berries per season. 5 families share it. Recently, total extraction hit 102, exceeding the sustainable yield.
scenario.text: Una hauls in a heavy load. 'If I leave these in the timber forest, someone else takes them tomorrow. At least this way my family eats.' The elder notes extraction is 22 crates of berries above sustainable levels.
scenario.speaker_context: Una follows individually rational logic that leads to collective depletion.

structure.pattern_description: A common-pool resource is rival but non-excludable. Each user captures full private benefit of extraction but bears only a fraction of the depletion cost, driving overuse.
structure.formal_form: Common-pool resource: rival, non-excludable. Private MB of extra extraction > private MC (shared 1/5). Each overextracts. Total > sustainable yield 80.
structure.why_wrong: Individual rationality drives overextraction. The problem is structural, not moral — the incentive system is misaligned.
structure.why_right: Recognizing the commons structure points toward solutions: property rights, catch limits, or community governance.
structure.counterpoint: Not all commons are doomed. Ostrom documented successful community governance of shared resources without privatization or centralized control.

assessment.identification_prompt: Each family benefits from taking more, but the timber forest is declining. What structural problem drives this?

assessment.identification_prompt: How does the incentive to cheat on commons agreements mirror the original problem? What enforcement mechanisms work?

structure.pattern_description: A common-pool resource is rival but non-excludable. Each user captures full private benefit of extraction but bears only a fraction of the depletion cost, driving overuse.
structure.formal_form: Compliance is a second-order public good: everyone benefits from enforcement but each prefers others bear the cost of monitoring. Solutions: peer monitoring, rotational inspection, graduated sanctions.
structure.why_wrong: Individual rationality drives overextraction. The problem is structural, not moral — the incentive system is misaligned.
structure.why_right: Recognizing the commons structure points toward solutions: property rights, catch limits, or community governance.
structure.counterpoint: Not all commons are doomed. Ostrom documented successful community governance of shared resources without privatization or centralized control.

scenario.context: Tormund and Maren in Thistlewood negotiate a trade of herbs for silver. Total surplus from trade: 46 gold. Tormund's outside option: 8 gold. Maren's outside option: 5 gold.
scenario.text: 'We agree the deal creates 46 gold in value. But I can walk away and get 8 from another buyer,' says Tormund. 'And I can get 5 elsewhere,' replies Maren. 'So how do we split the 46?'
scenario.speaker_context: Both understand surplus exists but need a principled way to divide it.

structure.pattern_description: Fair division depends on outside options, not just the total surplus. Better alternatives give more bargaining power.
structure.formal_form: Nash bargaining: remaining = 46 - 8 - 5 = 33. Split equally: Tormund gets 24.5, Maren gets 21.5.
structure.why_right: Bargaining theory prevents naive 50-50 splits and shows how outside options determine each party's fair share.
structure.counterpoint: Nash bargaining assumes equal power after outside options. In reality, patience, information, and social dynamics all matter.

assessment.identification_prompt: Surplus = 46, outside options = 8 and 5. What is a fair split?

rubric.description: Player suggests 50-50 without considering outside options.
Player recognizes outside options matter but cannot calculate.
Player accounts for floors but splits remainder incorrectly.
Player correctly applies Nash bargaining solution.
Player solves correctly and discusses how changing outside options shift power.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Each party's outside option is their guaranteed floor. Subtract both floors from the surplus. Split the remainder.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: If Tormund's outside option improves to 23, how does the split change?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Tormund is assertive; Maren is shrewd but fair.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: 'We both gain from this deal. But how much each of us gains — that is the question.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player solves the bargaining problem, both merchants accept and offer the player a commission on future trades.

scenario.context: Lady Einar in Silverpeak hired Tavish to manage her spice warehouse while she is away. Tavish receives 66 gold per month flat. Output fell 30% below expectations.
scenario.text: 'Tavish gets 66 gold whether the spice warehouse prospers or fails. I was in the capital and could not observe his effort. He had no reason to push himself,' says Einar.
scenario.speaker_context: Flat wage + unobservable effort = moral hazard.

structure.pattern_description: When a principal delegates to an agent whose effort is unobservable, the agent has rational incentive to shirk under flat pay. The problem is the incentive structure, not the person.
structure.formal_form: Agent payoff = 66 regardless of effort. Cost of effort = c(e) > 0. Agent minimizes cost by choosing minimum effort. Solutions: performance pay, monitoring, bonding.
structure.why_wrong: Flat wages make shirking rational. The contract structure, not character, drives the behavior.
structure.why_right: Recognizing the principal-agent structure leads to solutions: performance pay, monitoring, or bonding.
structure.counterpoint: Intrinsic motivation, reputation, and social norms can substitute for financial incentives. Not all agents shirk under flat pay.

assessment.identification_prompt: Why does the flat wage create a shirking incentive? How might Einar redesign the contract?

rubric.description: Player blames the agent's character.
Player senses the pay is wrong but cannot explain why.
Player identifies no incentive to work but proposes no solution.
Player identifies moral hazard and proposes incentive-compatible contract.
Player identifies moral hazard, proposes solutions, and distinguishes from adverse selection.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Tavish earns 66 whether output is high or low, what incentive does he have to work hard?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What are the trade-offs of performance pay? What happens if output falls due to bad luck, not shirking?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Einar is fair-minded; Tavish is capable when motivated.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: 'I do not want to fire Tavish. I want to fix the system.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player designs a better contract, output improves and Einar offers the player a consulting role.

scenario.context: The market master in Drifthollow posts grain supply and demand. Supply: Qs = 12*P. Demand: Qd = 68 - 8*P.
scenario.text:
The market master shows the board: Price | Supply | Demand
  1   |   12   |   60
  2   |   24   |   52
  3   |   36   |   44
  4   |   48   |   36
  5   |   60   |   28. 'Last week I set the price wrong and there were fights. Help me find the price where supply meets demand.'
scenario.speaker_context: The market master needs the equilibrium price.

structure.pattern_description: At equilibrium, quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. Prices above equilibrium create surpluses; prices below create shortages.
structure.why_right: The equilibrium price coordinates decentralized buyers and sellers. The market naturally adjusts toward the clearing price.
structure.counterpoint: Perfect competition, full information, and no externalities are assumed. Real markets may not clear due to frictions.

assessment.identification_prompt: Find the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded for grain.

rubric.description: Player cannot find where supply meets demand.
Player recognizes S and D should equal but guesses the price.
Player identifies equilibrium is nearby but cannot solve exactly.
Player correctly determines equilibrium P and Q.
Player solves correctly and explains the adjustment mechanism.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: At which price on the board are supply and demand closest? That is near equilibrium.

scenario.context: The grain market in Bellforge was in equilibrium at P*=5, Q*=75. Then a trade caravan doubles supply.
scenario.text: 'The market was balanced. Now a trade caravan doubles supply. Prices are moving and I cannot figure out where they will settle.'
scenario.speaker_context: A supply or demand shock shifts equilibrium.

structure.pattern_description: At equilibrium, quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. Prices above equilibrium create surpluses; prices below create shortages.
structure.formal_form: Shift the affected curve. New equilibrium at new intersection. Supply decrease → higher P, lower Q. Demand increase → higher P, higher Q. Etc.
structure.why_right: The equilibrium price coordinates decentralized buyers and sellers. The market naturally adjusts toward the clearing price.
structure.counterpoint: Perfect competition, full information, and no externalities are assumed. Real markets may not clear due to frictions.

scenario.context: The king decrees that bread in Larkhaven cannot sell above 4 gold. Equilibrium was P*=5, Q*=77. At 4: Qs=67, Qd=95.
scenario.text: 'The king means well, but at 4 gold, suppliers bring only 67 units while 95 want to buy. That is a shortage of 28. A black market is forming.'
scenario.speaker_context: Price ceiling below equilibrium creates shortage and deadweight loss.

structure.pattern_description: Binding price controls prevent the market from clearing. Ceilings create shortages; floors create surpluses. Both generate deadweight loss from unrealized trades.
structure.formal_form: Ceiling Pc=4 < P*=5. Qs(4)=67 < Qd(4)=95. Shortage=28. DWL = lost surplus from trades between Q=67 and Q=77.
structure.why_wrong: Price controls are well-intentioned but create predictable inefficiencies. The hidden cost is the trades that no longer occur.
structure.why_right: Understanding deadweight loss quantifies the cost of price controls, enabling comparison with alternative policies.
structure.counterpoint: If the equilibrium allocation is unjust, efficiency losses may be acceptable. Price controls may be defensible as second-best solutions.

assessment.identification_prompt: With a price ceiling of 4, what happens to the market? Who benefits and who is harmed?

scenario.context: The king decrees that flour in Brindlewood cannot sell above 5 gold. Equilibrium was P*=6, Q*=49. At 5: Qs=34, Qd=73.
scenario.text: 'The king means well, but at 5 gold, suppliers bring only 34 units while 73 want to buy. That is a shortage of 39. A black market is forming.'
scenario.speaker_context: Price ceiling below equilibrium creates shortage and deadweight loss.

structure.pattern_description: Binding price controls prevent the market from clearing. Ceilings create shortages; floors create surpluses. Both generate deadweight loss from unrealized trades.
structure.formal_form: Ceiling Pc=5 < P*=6. Qs(5)=34 < Qd(5)=73. Shortage=39. DWL = lost surplus from trades between Q=34 and Q=49.
structure.why_wrong: Price controls are well-intentioned but create predictable inefficiencies. The hidden cost is the trades that no longer occur.
structure.why_right: Understanding deadweight loss quantifies the cost of price controls, enabling comparison with alternative policies.
structure.counterpoint: If the equilibrium allocation is unjust, efficiency losses may be acceptable. Price controls may be defensible as second-best solutions.

assessment.identification_prompt: With a price ceiling of 5, what happens to the market? Who benefits and who is harmed?

scenario.context: Instead of a ceiling, the guild sets a price floor of 8 gold for medicine to protect producers. Qs at floor = 93, Qd = 66.
scenario.text: 'The guild says no one can sell below 8. Producers love it. But now there are 27 unsold units piling up.'
scenario.speaker_context: Price floor above equilibrium creates surplus and deadweight loss.

structure.pattern_description: Binding price controls prevent the market from clearing. Ceilings create shortages; floors create surpluses. Both generate deadweight loss from unrealized trades.
structure.formal_form: Floor Pf=8 > P*=7. Qs=93 > Qd=66. Surplus=27. Producers who sell gain; those who cannot sell, and all buyers, lose.
structure.why_wrong: Price controls are well-intentioned but create predictable inefficiencies. The hidden cost is the trades that no longer occur.
structure.why_right: Understanding deadweight loss quantifies the cost of price controls, enabling comparison with alternative policies.
structure.counterpoint: If the equilibrium allocation is unjust, efficiency losses may be acceptable. Price controls may be defensible as second-best solutions.

assessment.identification_prompt: A price floor of 8 creates what market outcome? Who gains, who loses?

scenario.context: The flour market in Brackenmoor has both a ceiling (to help buyers) and a subsidy (to compensate sellers). Is this better or worse than a simple ceiling? What about a simple subsidy without a ceiling?
scenario.text: 'The king caps the price AND pays sellers the difference. Clever? Or just a more expensive way to do the same thing?'
scenario.speaker_context: Comparing policy instruments: ceiling, subsidy, ceiling-plus-subsidy.

structure.pattern_description: Binding price controls prevent the market from clearing. Ceilings create shortages; floors create surpluses. Both generate deadweight loss from unrealized trades.
structure.formal_form: Ceiling: shortage + DWL. Subsidy alone: no shortage, higher quantity, government cost. Ceiling + subsidy: no shortage if subsidy covers gap, but fiscal cost. Subsidy alone typically more efficient than ceiling.
structure.why_wrong: Price controls are well-intentioned but create predictable inefficiencies. The hidden cost is the trades that no longer occur.
structure.why_right: Understanding deadweight loss quantifies the cost of price controls, enabling comparison with alternative policies.
structure.counterpoint: If the equilibrium allocation is unjust, efficiency losses may be acceptable. Price controls may be defensible as second-best solutions.

assessment.identification_prompt: Compare a price ceiling, a producer subsidy, and a ceiling with subsidy. Which achieves the equity goal at lowest efficiency cost?

scenario.context: Sigrid's sawmill in Coppergate earns 93 gold profit but causes noise and sawdust that costs nearby homes 30 gold in health problems.
scenario.text: '93 gold profit. Good business,' says Sigrid. But Iona from nearby homes says: 'We spend 30 gold on health problems. Sigrid does not pay for that.'
scenario.speaker_context: Sigrid's prices do not reflect the full social cost.

structure.pattern_description: An externality is a cost or benefit imposed on third parties not involved in the transaction. Negative externalities cause overproduction; positive externalities cause underproduction.
structure.formal_form: Private cost leads to 93 profit. Social cost adds 30. Social profit = 63. Market overproduces because price < social cost.
structure.why_wrong: Market prices send the wrong signal when externalities are present. The market 'works' only because it ignores third-party costs or benefits.
structure.why_right: Identifying externalities is essential for understanding market failure. Solutions: Pigouvian taxes/subsidies, regulation, Coasean bargaining, liability rules.
structure.counterpoint: Not all externalities require intervention. Small externalities with high transaction costs may be tolerable. The Coase theorem suggests negotiation can resolve some.

assessment.identification_prompt: What is the social cost of Sigrid's production? Why does the market get the quantity wrong?

rubric.description: Player sees no connection between the business and the harm.
Player recognizes harm but frames it as purely ethical.
Player identifies the cost imposition but not the market failure.
Player identifies the externality and explains over/under-production.
Player identifies, quantifies, and proposes internalization mechanisms.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Add Sigrid's cost and Iona's cost. That is the true social cost.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What if a tax of {external_cost} gold is levied on the {business}? What happens to output and the externality?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Sigrid is defensive; Iona is calm but firm.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: 'Sigrid is not breaking any law. But we are paying the price.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the externality and proposes a solution, the town council convenes to implement it.

scenario.context: The charcoal pit is the largest employer in Larkhaven. Taxing it would reduce pollution but might cause layoffs. The workers are also the ones breathing the dirty air. How do you weigh externality costs against employment?
scenario.text: 'Tax the charcoal pit and half the town loses work. Keep it open and they lose their health. Who decides which loss matters more?'
scenario.speaker_context: Externality policy has distributional consequences beyond efficiency.

structure.pattern_description: An externality is a cost or benefit imposed on third parties not involved in the transaction. Negative externalities cause overproduction; positive externalities cause underproduction.
structure.formal_form: Efficiency analysis: internalize the externality. Distributional analysis: who bears the cost of the policy? Transition costs, retraining, and compensation must be part of the design.
structure.why_wrong: Market prices send the wrong signal when externalities are present. The market 'works' only because it ignores third-party costs or benefits.
structure.why_right: Identifying externalities is essential for understanding market failure. Solutions: Pigouvian taxes/subsidies, regulation, Coasean bargaining, liability rules.
structure.counterpoint: Not all externalities require intervention. Small externalities with high transaction costs may be tolerable. The Coase theorem suggests negotiation can resolve some.

scenario.context: At the ships market in Havenport, sellers know the true quality but buyers cannot tell good from bad. Thane, a buyer, notices quality declining.
scenario.text: 'Ships used to be reliable here,' says Thane. 'Now good sellers go elsewhere because buyers offer average-quality prices. The market fills with junk, prices drop, more good sellers leave. It is a death spiral.'
scenario.speaker_context: Thane is describing the lemons problem.

structure.pattern_description: When one party knows more about quality than the other, the uninformed party offers average-quality prices, driving out high-quality goods.
structure.formal_form: Sellers know quality; buyers see only average. Buyers offer P = f(E[q]). Sellers with q > P withdraw. Average quality falls. P falls. Repeat.
structure.why_wrong: The market failure is caused by the information structure, not dishonesty. Even honest sellers cannot credibly communicate quality.
structure.why_right: Recognizing information asymmetry opens the door to solutions: warranties, certification, reputation systems, regulation.
structure.counterpoint: Not all markets with asymmetric information collapse. Reputation, return policies, and branding mitigate the problem.

assessment.identification_prompt: Why are good ships leaving the market? What drives the quality spiral?

rubric.description: Player blames dishonesty without seeing the information structure.
Player recognizes buyers cannot tell quality but misses the spiral.
Player identifies the information gap and seller withdrawal.
Player describes the adverse selection spiral completely.
Player identifies adverse selection and proposes institutional solutions.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If you sell a good ship, would you accept a price based on the average quality at this market?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: What institution could restore buyer confidence? Certification? Warranties?

game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: 'Something poisoned this market, and it was not the ships — it was the information.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the lemons problem, they help establish a certification system that restores market quality.

structure.pattern_description: When one party knows more about quality than the other, the uninformed party offers average-quality prices, driving out high-quality goods.
structure.formal_form: Signaling equilibrium: cost of signal < benefit for high-quality seller, > benefit for low-quality seller. Separating equilibrium: only good sellers signal.
structure.why_wrong: The market failure is caused by the information structure, not dishonesty. Even honest sellers cannot credibly communicate quality.
structure.why_right: Recognizing information asymmetry opens the door to solutions: warranties, certification, reputation systems, regulation.

scenario.context: Dagna runs a potion shop in Kingsford and has discovered that adding an overpriced option nobody buys to make the target look reasonable. They are testing it on customers.

scenario.speaker_context: Dagna has stumbled on decoy effect and is conflicted about the ethics.

structure.pattern_name: Behavioral economics: nudges and choice architecture
structure.pattern_description: People's choices are influenced by context, framing, and presentation, not just by rational preferences. Choice architecture is unavoidable.
structure.formal_form: Phenomenon: decoy effect. adding an overpriced option nobody buys to make the target look reasonable. People's choices are influenced by context and framing, not just by preferences and prices as rational-choice theory assumes.
structure.why_wrong: When used to exploit, nudges undermine autonomous decision-making. Customers believe they are choosing freely but are being steered.
structure.why_right: When used ethically, nudges improve outcomes. Choice architecture is unavoidable — designing it thoughtfully is better than leaving it to chance.
structure.counterpoint: Critics argue any deliberate framing is manipulative. The ethical line depends on whether the nudge serves the chooser or the designer.

scenario.context: A plague aftermath devastated Thornwall. Alderman Rowena claims it will boost the economy because weavers will earn 786 gold in repairs.
scenario.text: 'Weavers are going to earn a fortune! The plague aftermath is the best thing for business,' says Rowena. 'Every disaster is an opportunity.'
scenario.speaker_context: Rowena sees repair spending (the seen) but ignores what the money would have bought (the unseen).

structure.pattern_description: The fallacy counts visible repair spending as economic gain while ignoring the invisible alternative spending that the same money would have funded.
structure.formal_form: Seen: 786 gold in repair work. Unseen: 786 gold in investment, improvement, or consumption that would have occurred otherwise. Net effect = negative (value of destroyed assets lost).
structure.why_wrong: Destruction redirects spending from productive to restorative use. The seen (repair jobs) masks the unseen (forgone investment or consumption).
structure.counterpoint: In a depressed economy with idle resources, stimulus spending — including repair — can mobilize slack. But this is the Keynesian qualification, not a validation of the fallacy.

assessment.identification_prompt: Rowena says the plague aftermath is good for the economy. What is wrong with this argument?

rubric.description: Player agrees destruction creates prosperity.
Player senses something is wrong but cannot articulate it.
Player recognizes repair costs come from somewhere but misses the full logic.
Player identifies seen vs. unseen and the opportunity cost of repair spending.
Player identifies the fallacy, connects to opportunity cost, and notes the Keynesian exception.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The weavers get 786 gold. Where does that money come from? What would it have bought otherwise?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: After a real disaster, economic activity often rises. Does this mean the disaster helped?

structure.pattern_description: The error of assuming all interactions are zero-sum — that one party's gain must be another's loss — when voluntary trade creates new value for both parties.
